The project

My teammate and I competed as Literal Zero in IMC Prosperity 3. Across five rounds, the simulated market introduced new products and information, so each submission required another cycle of analysis, strategy development, and testing.

We combined regression, mean reversion, synthetic basket pricing, and options valuation. The team finished first in Central America and the Caribbean and third in Latin America. The public repository includes our submission and a candid account of what worked and what did not.

My role
Teammate; strategy research and implementation

Result

Different products, different signals

Regression and reversion

For Kelp, we used a linear regression based on recent prices. Rainforest Resin and Squid Ink led to market-making and mean-reversion strategies.

Synthetic baskets

Gift Basket prices were compared with the values of their underlying components. We traded deviations using a z-score, while recognizing that a large gap did not always produce a profitable trade.

Options and volatility

Black–Scholes helped recover implied volatility for Volcanic Rock vouchers. A fitted volatility curve informed mispricing signals, with delayed delta hedging and attention to gamma.

How it works

The work followed a recurring research loop: inspect the available historical data, turn a pricing hypothesis into a strategy, and test it before the submission window closed.

  1. Study the market

    Plot prices, spreads, and product relationships. Look for repeatable behavior in the available history.

  2. Build the strategy

    Translate the signal into Python trading logic and account for positions, hedging, and product-specific constraints.

  3. Test and submit

    Backtest the hypothesis, adjust assumptions, and submit to the competition’s simulated market.

The interactive chart above illustrates signal shapes; the competition write-up contains the actual research and round-by-round results.

A key decision

The failed round is part of the story.

In round four, we used sunlight and sugar-price relationships to trade Magnificent Macarons. The approach worked in backtests but proved overfit in the competition simulation.

That failure made the limits of historical fit concrete. A useful strategy needs a reason to survive beyond the data used to discover it, and the team write-up documents the setback alongside the stronger results.

The five rounds

Round 1

Market making, short-history regression, and a mean-reversion signal for Squid Ink.

Round 2

Gift Baskets compared against the synthetic value of their components.

Round 3

Options mispricing, implied volatility, and hedging for Volcanic Rock vouchers.

Round 4

A sunlight-based Macarons strategy that overfit the backtest.

Round 5

Trader-identity patterns used to find a Croissants signal.
